summary: An April 1st humor RFC suggesting new MIME types such as electronic staples and paper clips for tying documents together. It is a joke.

plainLanguage.summary: A pretend plan to invent electronic staples and paper clips to hold digital papers together. It was written as an April Fools Day prank.

subtitle: An April 1st parody of serious MIME type proposals.

tldr.problem: This RFC is not a real proposal but an April 1st joke.
tldr.mechanism: It humorously parodies formal MIME type registration RFCs by proposing fictional electronic staples and paper clips as new MIME types for binding documents.
tldr.outcome: It served as April Fools humor, but highlights the absurdity of over-engineering simple document association problems.

today: This is an April Fools RFC from 1 April 1996. It is informational and humorous, not a real proposal.

sections.title: The April Fools Joke
sections.content:
RFC 1927 is an April 1st joke document that parodies serious Internet standards proposals. It proposes new MIME types called electronic staples and electronic paper clips to bind groups of related documents in digital form, much like physical office supplies bind paper documents.

The author adopts the formal tone of a real RFC while describing increasingly absurd and impractical features, making fun of the tendency to over-engineer solutions to simple problems.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC pretends to propose electronic staples and paper clips to hold digital documents together. It is a joke from April Fools Day.

sections.title: Fictional Features
sections.content:
The proposal describes two MIME types: staples for permanent binding and paper clips for loose association. It then proposes increasingly elaborate features, including different sizes for hierarchical assembly, colored and shaped clips with customizable appearance via attributes like color=, shape= and src= for custom images.

The joke extends to suggesting that documents with electronic staples might be incompatible with high-speed copying programs, and proposing 3D modelling support for virtual reality headsets viewing customized paper clips.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke suggests fancy electronic staples and paper clips with colors, shapes, and even 3D models that could look different on your screen.

sections.title: The Satire
sections.content:
The document pokes fun at the complexity and patent concerns of Internet technology by proposing a billing system (via First Virtual) for using electronic staples, bulk purchasing schemes for staple boxes of 5000, and certificates to prevent counterfeiting of staples.

Later sections humorously address safety hazards, such as preventing electronic paper clips from being used on data destined for young children or from being attached to floppy disks where they might cause damage—issues that do not apply to digital objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke makes fun of how Internet standards sometimes add unnecessary complexity, cost, and complications to simple ideas.
